query: How do you stop people pleasing?
why_in_two_sentences: Berkeley's Greater Good is a reflective essay on authenticity-versus-safety whose only concrete tool is a five-step feel-your-emotion check-in, and Oprah's piece is personal narratives plus expert quotes with no structured how-to list. Ours locates the mechanism in the one-second gap before the automatic yes, gives seven concrete repetitions and a resolved-state table, and answers 30+ situation-specific FAQs.
what_the_winner_does_that_we_dont: Berkeley names the safety exception with a vivid scenario (a traffic stop where 'speaking your truth' is unwise) so the reader learns authenticity is not always the goal; ours flags safety but does not illustrate a low-stakes case where agreeing is the smart move
what_we_do_that_they_dont: Pinpoints the actual leverage point (the one-second gap between request and yes) and builds the whole method around delaying inside it with a scripted line: 'Let me check my week and come back to you tonight'

Gives seven ordered repetitions including 'speak first / name the restaurant before hearing theirs', 'let one person be mildly disappointed and stay in the room', 'skip the repair work afterward', and 'treat resentment as data pointing to a misplaced yes'
Provides the one-hour-later test to distinguish pleasing from genuine generosity (residue, private tally, flare of irritation)
Maps where it hides across five arenas (daily life, parents, own emotions, self-image, partner) with the sentence underneath each, plus a resolved-state Tuesday table
Separates recognition speed (weeks) from the flinch fading (months), and gives a clinical/safety boundary for coercive or unsafe relationships

above_the_fold.ours: H1 restates the query; the short-answer box names the gap-and-two-halves method in four sentences, then an identify-box of five first-person sentences; the reader gets a mechanism and a mirror, which earns the scroll.
above_the_fold.theirs: Berkeley opens mid-argument replying to commenters about a prior post on authenticity, which assumes context the searcher doesn't have and buries the payoff. Oprah opens with a first-person 'yes-woman' memoir that is engaging but slow to any actionable takeaway.

questions_they_answer_that_we_dont: When is it actually smart NOT to speak your truth?
Why does making others happy still leave people pleasers feeling empty?
trust_signals: Berkeley carries UC Berkeley's Greater Good Science Center authority and cites research (surface vs. deep acting), and Oprah quotes a named PhD author (Harriet Braiker); ours has a named founder byline (Florian Rolke) and first-person practitioner history but no external citations, winning on specificity of the practice rather than cited authority.
one_change_with_most_traffic_impact: Add a short 'when agreeing is actually the right call' block distinguishing wise accommodation from pattern-driven pleasing; it captures the reader worried that boundaries make them selfish or rude and pre-empts the objection both competitors address.
